stem: What is Prometheus's built-in expression browser mainly for?

options.note: Right. For lasting dashboards, use Grafana.
The docs point to Grafana (or console templates) for graphs and dashboards.
Routing is configured in Alertmanager.
The UI doesn't edit configuration.

explanation: The expression browser at /graph lets you enter any expression and see the result as a table or graph. It's primarily useful for ad-hoc queries and debugging.

stem: In the Prometheus UI, which tab runs an instant query and which runs a range query?

options.text: Table is an instant query; Graph is a range query
options.note: Right. Graph evaluates the expression at many steps over time.

options.text: Table is a range query; Graph is an instant query
options.note: Reversed.
Table shows one value per series at a single time.
A graph over time needs a range query.

explanation: In the Prometheus UI, the Table tab is for instant queries and the Graph tab is for range queries.
hint: Which one shows values over time?

stem: By default, which port does Grafana listen on?

options.note: Right. http://localhost:3000, default login admin/admin.
9090 is Prometheus's default port.
9093 is commonly Alertmanager.
9100 is the Node Exporter.

explanation: By default, Grafana listens on http://localhost:3000. The default login is admin/admin.
hint: Not one of the 9xxx Prometheus ports.

stem: What do you configure in Grafana so it can query Prometheus?

options.text: A Prometheus data source with the server URL, such as http://localhost:9090/
options.note: Right. Then Save & Test.

options.text: A scrape config pointing Grafana at your applications
options.note: Prometheus scrapes. Grafana queries Prometheus.
Grafana reads through the Prometheus HTTP API, not remote write.
Receivers are for notifications.

explanation: To create a Prometheus data source in Grafana: add a data source, select Prometheus, set the server URL (for example http://localhost:9090/), then Save & Test.
hint: Grafana needs to know where Prometheus is.

sources.title: Grafana › Creating a Prometheus data source

stem: A panel query returns series with method and status labels. Which Grafana legend format shows them as "GET - 200"?

options.note: Right. That's the docs' own example.
Grafana's Prometheus legend format uses double curly braces.
That's Prometheus alert templating, not Grafana legend format.
That would print the literal words.

explanation: To format legend names, use the Legend format input, for example {{method}} - {{status}}.
hint: Label names in double curly braces.

stem: What does the Grafana documentation linked from the Prometheus docs recommend using inside rate() and increase() in panels (Grafana 7.2+)?

options.note: Right. It picks a sensible window for the panel's resolution.
Too short. It would often contain fewer than two samples.
That isn't the recommendation.
rate() requires a range vector.

explanation: In Grafana 7.2 and later, the $__rate_interval variable is recommended for use in the rate and increase functions.
hint: Grafana provides a variable for this.

stem: A dashboard panel shows http_requests_total as an ever-rising line. What's the better query for a traffic panel?

options.note: Right. Show the per-second rate, not the cumulative total.
That's the same rising total, just shifted back in time.
Still the cumulative value, not traffic.
deriv is for gauges and ignores counter resets.

explanation: Raw counters are rarely useful. Use rate() to get the per-second rate at which they increase.

stem: You're exploring an unfamiliar metric and might build a dashboard from it. What do the docs advise?

options.text: Start in the table view until the result is reasonable (hundreds, not thousands, of series), then graph
options.note: Right. Graphing a huge result can time out or overload the server or browser.

options.text: Always graph immediately with a 30-day range
options.note: That's the fastest way to overload things.
That selects every series in the database.

options.text: Avoid aggregating, so you see raw data
options.note: Filtering and aggregating is exactly what keeps results manageable.

explanation: When building queries over unknown data, start in the tabular view until the result set is reasonable (hundreds, not thousands, of series). Only switch to graph mode once you've filtered or aggregated enough.

sources.title: Querying basics › Avoiding slow queries and overloads

stem: A dashboard viewed by 50 people runs an expensive query on every refresh. What helps most?

options.text: A recording rule that precomputes the expression, with the panel querying the recorded series
options.note: Right. Recording rules are especially useful for dashboards.
That reduces data resolution but doesn't remove the query cost.
That doesn't make an expensive query cheap.
Alertmanager doesn't serve dashboard queries.

explanation: Recording rules precompute frequently needed or expensive expressions. This is especially useful for dashboards, which query the same expression every time they refresh.

sources.title: Querying basics › Avoiding slow queries and overloads

stem: Where can you find pre-built Grafana dashboards for common systems?

options.text: The shared dashboard collection on grafana.com, imported via Dashboards → Import
options.note: Right. Filter by the Prometheus data source and fix the datasource entries.
Exporters expose metrics, not dashboards.
Alertmanager doesn't host dashboards.
It doesn't.

explanation: Grafana.com maintains a collection of shared dashboards that can be downloaded and imported into your Grafana.
hint: The vendor's website hosts a library.

stem: What changed for console templates in Prometheus 3.0?

options.text: They're no longer bundled, so you supply your own via --web.console.templates and --web.console.libraries
options.note: Right. The docs suggest newcomers try Grafana first anyway.

options.text: They became the default dashboard UI
options.note: The opposite. They were unbundled.
They're served by Prometheus, unrelated to Grafana.
3.0 stopped bundling them.

explanation: Starting with Prometheus 3.0, console templates and libraries are no longer bundled. To use them you provide your own via the --web.console.templates and --web.console.libraries flags.
hint: Check the caution at the top of the console templates page.
